Lesson 6 · Anticipate next week

Which stores will need attention next week?

We have described store differences and fitted relationships. The director now asks for a weekly list of stores that are likely to struggle before the next stock report arrives.

Baseline only · targets in weeks 3–16 · no alerts yet

Method in this decision: Prediction and validation

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The decision brief

The operations team has limited review capacity. At the end of each week, it wants to identify stores that deserve attention during the following week. The target is next week’s stockout rate. A useful forecast must arrive before that week starts and beat a simple planning rule on later observations. The team will compare a regression with a small decision tree, select a procedure on a validation period, and then evaluate it on a final untouched period.

Specify the output and the cost of a miss

Define the task before choosing an algorithm

The requested output determines the task
Output neededPrediction taskRetail use
A numerical stockout rateRegressionPlan the expected review burden
A category such as above targetClassificationChoose which stores receive a review
A probability of missing the targetProbability estimationCombine risk with the cost of action

Name the prediction unit, target period, available inputs, and action. The course’s main target is a numerical rate for a store next week. A threshold can later turn that forecast into a queue, but the capacity rule and the accuracy measure remain separate choices.

Choose a loss that reflects the decision

MAE = mean |actual − prediction|; MSE = mean (actual − prediction)²

RMSE is the square root of MSE. Squared loss gives especially large misses more influence. If missing a severe stockout problem is costlier than an unnecessary review, an asymmetric decision loss may be appropriate. State those costs before comparing models, and evaluate candidate procedures on the same observations.

Complexity changes both bias and variability

  • Underfitting: the model misses useful structure.
  • Overfitting: the model follows development-sample noise.
  • Irreducible variation: next week contains information unavailable today.

Expected prediction error is often discussed as squared bias, variance, and irreducible error. A more flexible model can reduce approximation bias while making the fitted procedure less stable. The purpose of validation is to observe the net effect on later, unused outcomes.

Put every input on the decision clock

At the end of week 13, staff know week 13’s stockout rate, each store’s usual delivery time, its urban location, and the promotion plan for week 14. A demand forecast for week 14 is also available. These are the five model inputs. The demand actually observed in week 14 arrives too late for that forecast.

The lag_rate column means the previous week’s rate. Its name matters: using the same week’s outcome would allow the model to read its answer. Weeks 1–16 contain no alerts, so the forecasting exercise describes operations before the policy changes. The later treatment flag is excluded from the input list.

The forecast input contract
FieldAvailable when the forecast is made
lag_rateAt the end of the previous week
lead_days, urbanStore attributes already known
demand_forecastPlanning forecast for the target week
promotion_planScheduled before the target week

Let later weeks choose the forecasting rule

Fit candidates on target weeks 3–10 (1,200 observations). Compare their forecasts for weeks 11–13 (450 observations). The final period is weeks 14–16, containing 450 observations. Every split follows time, so each evaluation asks the model to predict a later period.

Regression combines the five inputs in an additive equation. The small tree divides stores into a few groups with different predicted rates. Both are judged using the same root-mean-square error: square each prediction miss, average the squared misses, and take a square root. Large misses receive extra weight, and the result remains in percentage points.

Choose on weeks 11–13
CandidateValidation RMSE (percentage points)
Linear regression2.78
Small tree3.05

The selected rule is Linear regression. Fit that procedure again using weeks 3–13, then freeze it before opening weeks 14–16. The mean-rate baseline is also learned from weeks 3–13.

Use repeated, time-ordered checks during development

Move the validation window forward

Rolling validation within development weeks 3–13
Training target weeksValidation target weeks
3–78–9
3–910–11
3–1112–13

Ordinary k-fold validation fits on all but one fold and scores the held-out fold. For this weekly decision, preserve time instead: each validation window follows its training period. The final weeks 14–16 remain outside model tuning. Fit preprocessing, including scaling or imputation, using each fold’s training rows only.

Training criteria and validation answer different questions

Same development rows; *common likelihood constants omitted
Model degreeParametersTraining RMSEAIC*BIC*
162.783383.793416.25
2212.753377.973491.55

AIC and BIC penalize likelihood-based training fit for complexity. Here the Gaussian-error forms use n log(RSS/n) plus 2k or k log(n). They are comparable across these models because the outcome and observations are the same. Later-period prediction loss remains the direct check for the operating task.

Preprocessing belongs inside the fitted procedure

  • Define features from information available at the decision time.
  • Fit missing-value rules and scaling on training data.
  • Apply those rules unchanged to validation and test rows.
  • Keep target coding and category reference levels aligned.

A missing-value indicator can preserve information that a field was unavailable. An imputed value needs a stated rule; it is not a recovered observation. In this case the five forecast inputs are complete, so no imputation is needed. The important principle is that future observations must not influence the preparation of past training data.

RMSE = square root of the mean squared miss across all 450 final store-weeks

The simple baseline scores 3.88 percentage points; the frozen model scores 2.96. The table shows how each row contributes to that score. Averaging only these five displayed rows would describe that extract; the reported score uses every final row.

During the final period, the model stays fixed but each weekly forecast receives the latest available previous-week rate. This is the operating routine we intend to run: update the inputs each week, not the fitted model after every outcome.

Prediction accuracy is an operational intermediate result. To use the score, the team still chooses how many stores it can review and what an intervention costs. The forecast helps prioritize that capacity. The next lesson asks whether the proposed alert itself improves the outcome.

Ask whether a smaller predictive model is useful

LASSO adds a cost for large coefficients

Minimize mean squared loss / 2 + α × Σ|slope coefficients|

As the penalty α increases, coefficients shrink and some become exactly zero. The intercept is not penalized. Standardize the candidate predictors so a coefficient’s penalty does not depend merely on whether its field is measured in days or index points. Retained coefficients describe this fitted prediction procedure, not causal importance.

The candidate features are the five timely inputs plus their degree-two terms and interactions. Rolling validation selects α=0.01. Refit that procedure on weeks 3–13, then evaluate it once on the final period. This extends the original regression-versus-tree exercise with a pre-specified regularized procedure.

This final comparison reports the performance of fixed procedures; it does not retune them using the test outcomes. When a small error difference competes with complexity, consider reproducibility, maintenance, and how often the model will be refitted.

A log prediction needs an explicit return to business units

If predicted log Y = ln(10): exp(prediction) = 10; residual-adjusted mean = 10.20

This arithmetic illustration uses log residuals −0.2 and +0.2. Exponentiating the mean log outcome does not generally give the mean outcome, because exponentiation is nonlinear. A residual smearing factor averages exp(residual). Compare transformed-target procedures using the same original-scale loss that matters for the decision, and establish how zeros are handled before taking logs.

Close the loop after deployment

  • Record the inputs, forecast, model version, and action taken.
  • Monitor prediction error and operating cost over time.
  • Check whether store conditions or data definitions have changed.
  • Set a review date and a rule for refitting or retiring the model.

A model trained on historical operations depends on a sufficiently stable relationship when deployed. New promotions, a changed monitoring basket, or the alert policy itself can change that relationship. Monitoring makes the forecast an operating process with an owner.

Turn the forecast into a review queue

Use the predicted ranking to prepare a review list before the week begins. Store managers record which products need action, how much time the review takes, and whether the information was useful. A review list is a capacity choice: raising the cutoff reduces workload while leaving more stores to normal operations.

Carry two things into the pilot proposal: a forecasting procedure with a demonstrated evaluation period, and an explicit operational action that an alert recipient should take. A good forecast identifies a problem; the trial will measure what the response changes.

Update the decision memo

Forecast procedure selected by time: Linear regression; final RMSE 2.96 percentage points versus 3.88 for the mean-rate rule. Use it to prepare a review queue, then evaluate the alert action separately.

Make the call

The observed week 14 demand improves the score. Should it replace the week 14 demand forecast as an input?

Compare your reasoning

Use the forecast available before week 14. Actual week 14 demand is learned during the target period and would change the timing of the business decision being evaluated.

The bigger picture

Prediction joins data analysis to a recurring decision. The important chain is information available now, a forecast for later, a capacity rule, and an action someone can take. Testing that whole sequence on later weeks gives operations a procedure it can actually repeat.

After your decision: open the known answer

Future demand and shelf availability contain new random variation. The generator stores that variation, but the five forecast inputs expose only information available at the weekly decision time.
